newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels say ball now in government court.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say ball now in government court.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima called on world opinion on Thursday to press for a bloodless end to the country's 16-day stand-off and said the ball was now in the government's court.

"We ask the progressive men and women of the world to continue demanding of the Peruvian government a political solution which will bring the freedom of (rebel) political prisoners and the prisoners of war taken by our commando unit," the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement said in a statement.
"It is the Peruvian government's turn to speak."

The communique, from "somewhere in the central jungle" of Peru, reached news media after the release on Wednesday of seven more hostages by the rebels but appeared to have been written at the end of December.

The government of President Alberto Fujimori, still angered by an impromptu news conference given by the rebels inside the compound on New Year's Eve, did not send negotiator Domingo Palermo to receive the seven freed men and remained silent on the stand-off.

Both sides have waged a propaganda battle throughout the crisis. The government has cut off the residence's communication links and mostly kept journalists two blocks away from the compound, while the MRTA has used methods from cardboard placards to the Internet to get their demands across.

The seven released on Wednesday were four Japanese businessmen and three Peruvians, including a top privatisation official, Juan Assereto. All of them appeared in good health as they strolled out of the Japanese ambassador's residence clutching plastic bags containing dirty clothes.
The release did little to change the overall balance of the hostage crisis, with the MRTA rebels sticking to their original demand that the government pardon about 400 jailed comrades.

They still held 74 hostages whom they consider to be the most valuable -- including high-ranking government officials and military top brass, two foreign ambassadors and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is also among the hostages, was furious at the rebels' Tuesday propaganda coup and spent New Year's Day cloistered at Government Palace with security advisers.
"He's annoyed and wouldn't you be? They took the initiative and made a mockery of him, managing to send their faces around the world in minutes," a palace source told Reuters.

Dressed in combat gear and carrying an automatic rifle, Nestor Cerpa, leader of the 20-odd rebels who stormed a party at the residence on Dec. 17, held court for about two hours on Tuesday after reporters slipped into the compound, and harangued Fuijimori's government as a "dictatorship."
Cerpa reiterated that the rebels would not surrender until their prisoners had been released and said he was in no hurry to end the standoff.
He added, however, that the doors of the residence were open to government negotiators and said he was willing to consider mediation by Cuba or Russia.
Fujimori has flatly rejected the rebels' demands, though he has said "several options" were being looked at to try to end the crisis. His government says the MRTA are "terrorists."
An MRTA spokesman told Reuters the rebels would swap their hostages for the liberation of some of their jailed comrades.

"Our original and central demand is the release of comrades in jail, and an exchange of the prisoners of war is one obvious way to achieve this," MRTA member Isaac Velazco told Reuters in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.

Wednesday's releases again coincided with the presence of Peruvian Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani at the residence. Diplomatic sources have speculated that Cipriani, a close personal friend of Fujimori, has taken on an important negotiating role in the crisis, something Cipriani has publicly denied.
While Fujimori maintained a rigid silence, the man whose birthday the ill-fated reception was celebrating expressed his deep concern for the remaining hostages.
"My heart hurts deeply when I think of those who cannot celebrate the New Year with their families," Japanese Emperor Akihito was quoted as saying by Yomiuri Shimbun.
In Lima hundreds carrying flags and banners joined a peace march on Wednesday through the streets shouting, "Free the hostages! The people want peace!"
